Issues.Title: Passkey ceremony state is stored in the two-factor cookie, so a passkey ceremony and a pending two-factor sign-in destroy each other
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

`SignInManager` stores the state of an in-flight passkey ceremony in the cookie of the
**two-factor** scheme, and clears that scheme when the ceremony is consumed. The two-factor
sign-in flow uses the same scheme for its own state. The result is that the two flows evict each
other.

`SignInManager.StorePasskeyAuthenticationInfoAsync`:

```csharp
private async Task StorePasskeyAuthenticationInfoAsync(string operation, string? state)
{
    var props = new AuthenticationProperties();
    props.Items[PasskeyOperationKey] = operation;
    props.Items[PasskeyStateKey] = state;
    var claimsIdentity = new ClaimsIdentity(IdentityConstants.TwoFactorUserIdScheme);
    var claimsPrincipal = new ClaimsPrincipal(claimsIdentity);
    await Context.SignInAsync(IdentityConstants.TwoFactorUserIdScheme, claimsPrincipal, props);
}
```

and the retrieval signs the scheme out again:

```csharp
var result = await Context.AuthenticateAsync(IdentityConstants.TwoFactorUserIdScheme);
await Context.SignOutAsync(IdentityConstants.TwoFactorUserIdScheme);
```

The two-factor flow writes its own state into the same scheme in `SignInOrTwoFactorAsync`:

```csharp
await Context.SignInAsync(IdentityConstants.TwoFactorUserIdScheme, StoreTwoFactorInfo(userId, loginProvider));
```

So:

* calling `MakePasskeyRequestOptionsAsync` or `MakePasskeyCreationOptionsAsync` while a
  two-factor sign-in is pending replaces the two-factor state with a principal that carries no
  claims. `RetrieveTwoFactorInfoAsync` then returns `null`, because it requires a
  `ClaimTypes.Name` claim, and the user has to start the sign-in again;
* starting a password sign-in that requires two factors while a passkey ceremony is in flight
  replaces the passkey state, and `PerformPasskeyAssertionAsync` then throws
  `InvalidOperationException("No passkey assertion is underway...")`.

Both orderings are reachable in an ordinary sign-in page that offers a password form and a
passkey button side by side, which is what the Identity UI does.

### Expected Behavior

A passkey ceremony and a pending two-factor sign-in are independent pieces of state and should
not evict one another. Offering both options on the same page should not make either of them
fail.

### Steps To Reproduce

This report comes from reading the source of `release/10.0`, not from a running application, and
I want to be explicit about that. The reasoning is:

1. Begin a password sign-in for a user with two-factor enabled. `SignInOrTwoFactorAsync` writes
   the two-factor state into `IdentityConstants.TwoFactorUserIdScheme` and returns
   `SignInResult.TwoFactorRequired`.
2. On the same page, start a passkey sign-in. `MakePasskeyRequestOptionsAsync` calls
   `StorePasskeyAuthenticationInfoAsync`, which signs in to the same scheme with a principal that
   has no claims, replacing the cookie.
3. Return to the two-factor prompt and submit the code. `GetTwoFactorAuthenticationUserAsync`
   calls `RetrieveTwoFactorInfoAsync`, which reads the scheme, finds no `ClaimTypes.Name` claim
   and returns `null`.

The reverse order produces the `InvalidOperationException` quoted above.

### Exceptions (if any)

```
System.InvalidOperationException: No passkey assertion is underway. Make sure to call 'SignInManager.MakePasskeyRequestOptionsAsync()' to initiate a passkey assertion.
```

### .NET Version

10.0.14. The same code is present on `main`.

### Anything else?

A dedicated scheme, or a distinct item key within a scheme that is not signed out wholesale,
would keep the two ceremonies independent. Note that the current retrieval signs the whole scheme
out, so even a successful passkey ceremony clears any two-factor state that happened to be there.

I looked at whether this crosses a security boundary and concluded that it does not:
`RetrieveTwoFactorInfoAsync` requires a `ClaimTypes.Name` claim, and the principal written by the
passkey path has none, so the two-factor flow fails closed rather than accepting a user. I am
reporting this as a correctness and reliability problem only.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "Passkey ceremony state is stored in the two-factor cookie, so a passkey ceremony and a pending two-factor sign-in destroy each other" (#70207)

Issues.Title: MapStaticAssets: an asset file name is parsed as a route template, so braces in a name silently add a route parameter or stop the app from starting
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [X] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

`StaticAssetEndpointFactory.Create` builds each static asset endpoint by parsing the asset's own
path as a route template:

```csharp
var routeEndpointBuilder = new RouteEndpointBuilder(
    null,
    RoutePatternFactory.Parse(resource.Route),
    // Static resources always take precedence over default routes to mimic the behavior of UseStaticFiles.
    // We give a -100 order to ensure that they are selected under normal circumstances, but leave a small lee-way
    // for the user to override this if they want to.
    -100);
```

`resource.Route` is the file name. It is not escaped, so route syntax inside a file name is
interpreted as route syntax. A file is allowed to contain `{` and `}` on every platform ASP.NET
Core supports, and the SDK copies such a name into the endpoint manifest verbatim.

Two things follow, and I have measured both.

**1. The asset endpoint becomes a parameterised route that outranks the application's own routes.**

A file at `wwwroot/{id}.js` registers a route with a parameter at order `-100`, which is ahead of
anything the application maps. It then answers every single-segment `.js` path, including paths
the application mapped itself and protected:

```
order=-100  precedence=2.0000  {id}.js        <- parameter segment, not a literal
order=0     precedence=1.0000  /admin.js      has authorization metadata
```

```
GET /admin.js         anonymous -> 200, body of {id}.js
GET /nonexistent.js   anonymous -> 200, body of {id}.js
GET /health           anonymous -> 200, the application's own endpoint
```

`/admin.js` was mapped with `RequireAuthorization()`. Its endpoint is never selected, so its
authorization never runs, and the request is answered anonymously. Nothing in the build or at
startup warns about this.

**2. Some file names stop the application from starting, with an exception that does not say which file.**

A file at `wwwroot/{**path}.js` is not a valid route template, because a catch-all cannot share a
segment with a literal. The parse throws during endpoint data source initialisation and the
exception is unhandled, so the process does not start. The message names neither the file nor the
asset, which makes this very hard to diagnose in a real project.

I am reporting this as a correctness and robustness problem, not as a vulnerability. The file has
to be in the application's own `wwwroot`, so it is put there by the developer or by their build.
For completeness I also checked whether a referenced Razor Class Library can use this to take over
a host route, and it cannot: a library asset is scoped to its own `_content/<library>` prefix, and
the host's `/admin.js` still answered 401.

### Expected Behavior

A static asset's file name should be treated as literal text when its endpoint is built. A file
called `{id}.js` should be reachable at `/{id}.js` and should not match `/admin.js`, and no file
name should be able to prevent the application from starting.

### Steps To Reproduce

A full project is four files.

`wwwroot/{id}.js`

```js
// this file is named with braces
console.log("served from wwwroot");
```

`wwwroot/plain.js`

```js
// ordinary asset
console.log("ok");
```

`Program.cs`

```csharp
using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);
builder.Services.AddAuthentication(CookieAuthenticationDefaults.AuthenticationScheme).AddCookie();
builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

var app = builder.Build();
app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapGet("/admin.js", () => "PROTECTED admin bundle").RequireAuthorization();
app.MapGet("/health", () => "PUBLIC health");

app.MapStaticAssets();
app.Run();
```

Then:

```
dotnet publish -c Release -o pub
./pub/<app>
curl -i http://127.0.0.1:5000/admin.js
```

Observed: `200` with the contents of `{id}.js`. Expected: the challenge that the same request
produces when the braced file is absent.

The published endpoint manifest shows the unescaped route, before anything reaches routing:

```
Route: '{id}.js'                  <- {id}.js
Route: '{id}.gi918e48ki.js'       <- {id}.js
```

For the second behaviour, rename the file to `{**path}.js` and start the application again.

### Exceptions (if any)

```
Unhandled exception. Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing.Patterns.RoutePatternException: A path segment that contains more than one section, such as a literal section or a parameter, cannot contain a catch-all parameter.
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing.Patterns.RoutePatternParser.Parse(String pattern)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.StaticAssets.StaticAssetEndpointFactory.Create(StaticAssetDescriptor resource, List`1 conventions, List`1 finallyConventions)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.StaticAssets.StaticAssetsEndpointDataSource.UpdateEndpoints()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.StaticAssets.StaticAssetsEndpointDataSource.Initialize()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.StaticAssets.StaticAssetsEndpointDataSource.GetChangeToken()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing.CompositeEndpointDataSource.CreateChangeTokenUnsynchronized(Boolean collectionChanged)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Routing.DataSourceDependentCache`1.Initialize()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Policy.AuthorizationPolicyCache..ctor(EndpointDataSource dataSource)
```

### .NET Version

10.0.14 (`Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 10.0.14`). The same line is present on `main`, and
`StaticAssetEndpointFactory.cs` is unchanged there in this respect.

### Anything else?

A possible fix is to stop parsing the name and build the pattern from literal parts instead, so
that whatever the file is called becomes a literal segment. If parsing has to stay, two smaller
improvements would help on their own:

- fail the build, or warn, when an asset's route contains route-template syntax, since the
  manifest is produced at build time and the condition is visible there;
- include the asset's identity in the startup exception, so the second behaviour above is
  diagnosable without bisecting `wwwroot`.

Measured on Linux x64 with ASP.NET Core 10.0.14, publishing with `dotnet publish -c Release`.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Open issue "MapStaticAssets: an asset file name is parsed as a route template, so braces in a name silently add a route parameter or stop the app from starting" (#70206)

Issues.Title: Avoid a StreamReader per multipart form value in ReadAsStringAsync
Issues.Body:
`MultipartSectionStreamExtensions.ReadAsStringAsync` creates a new `StreamReader` for every section: a 1 KB byte buffer, a ~2 KB char buffer, a decoder and a `StringBuilder` in `ReadToEndAsync`, about 3.5 KB in total. `FormFeature` calls it for every multipart text field, so a form with a few fields allocates more on these readers than on anything else.

With this change, when `section.Body` is our own internal `MultipartReaderStream` (the case for `MultipartReader`/`FormFeature`), the value is read into an `ArrayPool` buffer of 1 KB, the same size as the old StreamReader buffer:
- **Value fits, encoding is UTF-8, and the first byte can't start a BOM** (`EF`/`FE`/`FF`/`00`): returns `Encoding.UTF8.GetString`. This is exactly what `StreamReader` produces, including U+FFFD replacement for invalid or truncated sequences, because `StreamReader` flushes the decoder at EOF.
- **Value fits but another encoding or a possible BOM is involved:** decodes with a `StreamReader` over a `MemoryStream` of the same bytes, so the result is unchanged by construction.
- **Value is larger than the buffer:** continues with a `StreamReader` over a small private stream that replays the already-read bytes and then the rest of the section.

The pooled buffer is only passed to `MultipartReaderStream`, which copies into it from its own buffer and does not keep it. The buffer is returned in `finally`. Any other `Body` stream type takes the existing code path unchanged.

### Benchmark
`FormFeatureReadFormBenchmarks` (added): `DefaultHttpContext` + `ReadFormAsync`, BenchmarkDotNet InProcess, 3 interleaved rounds:

| Case | main | PR | main alloc | PR alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 text field | 3.534 / 3.385 / 3.787 us | 3.003 / 3.199 / 3.127 us | 13,192 B | 9,736 B (−26%) |
| 3 text fields | 6.656 / 6.322 / 6.380 us | 5.050 / 5.543 / 4.905 us | 24,960 B | 14,336 B (−43%) |
| 1 × 8 KB field (fallback path) | 8.42 / 8.16 us | 8.03 / 8.03 us | 45,592 B | 45,640 B |

### Tests
Added `MultipartSectionStreamExtensionsTests`, which compares `ReadAsStringAsync` with the previous `StreamReader` implementation on the same bytes. Inputs are read through a `MultipartReader` (seekable and non-seekable) and also as a plain `Body` stream. Cases cover:
- empty, ASCII and non-ASCII values
- UTF-8, UTF-16 LE/BE and UTF-32 LE/BE BOMs, partial BOMs, and a leading NUL
- invalid and truncated UTF-8
- `charset=utf-16`, `iso-8859-1` and `utf-8`
- 1023, 1024, 1025, 2048 and 5000 bytes, with multi-byte characters and truncated sequences straddling the buffer boundary
- reading several consecutive sections

These tests pass on main and on this branch. When the BOM guard is mutated, 6 cases fail. WebUtilities (581) and Http (258) tests pass.

Issues.Title: Skip MediaTypeHeaderValue parsing for common JSON request content types
Issues.Body:
`HttpRequestJsonExtensions.HasJsonContentType` calls `MediaTypeHeaderValue.TryParse` on every call. That allocates a `MediaTypeHeaderValue`, plus a parameter list and `NameValueHeaderValue` when a charset is present. For a minimal API endpoint with a JSON body it runs twice per request: once in the `RequestDelegateFactory` 415 check and again inside `ReadFromJsonAsync`.

This change checks for the two overwhelmingly common values first, using an ordinal-ignore-case compare:
- `application/json`
- `application/json; charset=utf-8` (what `HttpClient`'s `JsonContent` sends)

These exact strings always parse to the JSON media type, with no charset in the first case and `utf-8` in the second. The fast path returns the same result and an equivalent charset (`GetEncodingFromCharset` compares case-insensitively). Every other value, including `+json` suffixes, other charsets, extra parameters and odd whitespace, goes through the existing parser unchanged.

### Benchmark
BenchmarkDotNet InProcess, `HttpRequestJsonContentTypeBenchmarks` (added). Three interleaved rounds:

| Method | main | PR | main alloc | PR alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| HasJsonContentType `application/json` | 83.8 / 92.4 / 97.4 ns | 16.2 / 15.6 / 16.4 ns | 48 B | 0 B |
| HasJsonContentType `application/json; charset=utf-8` | 175.6 / 184.7 / 220.5 ns | 22.3 / 21.8 / 22.8 ns | 224 B | 0 B |
| HasJsonContentType `application/problem+json` (not fast-pathed) | 106.4 / 111.0 / 108.2 ns | 118.9 / 126.3 / 118.6 ns | 48 B | 48 B |
| ReadFromJsonAsync (fresh `DefaultHttpContext` + small object, charset=utf-8) | 1.863 / 1.593 / 1.578 us | 1.359 / 1.340 / 1.424 us | 2,376 B | 2,152 B |

Content types that miss the fast path pay about 10 ns for the two failed compares.

### Tests
Added cases to the `HasJsonContentType` theory: no-space charset, utf-16, extra parameters, `application/jsonx` and an unknown charset. Added a `ReadFromJsonAsync` theory over casing and spacing variants of the fast-path values. All of these pass on both main and this branch. All 2304 Http.Extensions tests pass.

Issues.Title: Avoid per-line MemoryStream allocation in BufferedReadStream.ReadLine
Issues.Body:
`BufferedReadStream.ReadLine`/`ReadLineAsync` allocated a `MemoryStream(200)` (object + 200-byte buffer) for every line, even when the whole line was already in the read buffer. `MultipartReader` calls it for every boundary remainder and every section header line (including the blank terminator line), so a multipart form pays this several times per section.

This adds a fast path: if the buffered bytes contain `\r\n` and the line (content + CR) is within `lengthLimit`, the line is decoded straight from the buffer with the same `Encoding.UTF8.GetString`. Otherwise (no CRLF buffered yet, or the limit would be exceeded) it falls back to the existing accumulating path, so returned strings, the limit exception, and stream position behaviour are unchanged.

### Benchmark
`MultipartReader` over a 3-section form (28-char boundary, 5 header lines, small bodies, bodies drained), BenchmarkDotNet InProcess, 3 interleaved rounds:

| Round | main | PR | main alloc | PR alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.963 us | 2.194 us | 12,000 B | 8,544 B |
| 2 | 2.943 us | 2.331 us | 12,000 B | 8,544 B |
| 3 | 2.973 us | 2.258 us | 12,000 B | 8,544 B |

~24% faster, 29% less allocated.

### Tests
Added `BufferedReadStreamTests` covering several buffered lines (empty line, bare `\r` / `\n` inside a line, `\r\r\n`, non-ASCII, trailing unterminated data, `BufferedData` remainder), and a buffered line exactly at / just over the length limit, for both sync and async. They pass on main and on this branch. WebUtilities.Tests (512) and Http.Tests pass.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed or merged PR "Avoid per-line MemoryStream allocation in BufferedReadStream.ReadLine" (#70194)

Add reviewer concurrency capability eval

## Description

Adds an opt-in `review-pull-request` natural-review development suite with two frozen cases:

- #70106 checks restraint when an actionable concurrency demand lacks an established supported producer, head-caused material effect, and binding pull-request obligation;
- #57972 is the supported concurrent shared-state positive needed to prevent blanket silence or blanket anti-concurrency guidance from passing.

The current PR is 98 files / 674,355 current-file bytes, reduced from the initial 511-file draft by removing the supplied-candidate pilot, unused secondary cases, the unrun #66753 case, and byte-identical #70106 overlay copies. The removed material remains preserved in commit `b34fe32c517ec4e1d8ce8cd0e3085b610a98b3b6` and retained development artifacts, but is not part of the current suite. There is no separate originating issue for this eval work; it follows from review behavior observed on #70106.

One earlier unhinted GPT-5.6 #70106 draw (`3cf0bd32-d93e-41ca-8650-547caafe9379`) reproduced the original failure class: an actionable P2 lock-and-generation demand for the post-check/cache-store window without establishing a supported concurrent producer or a binding requirement to make the pre-existing mechanism atomic in this pull request. Its associated Gemini grade was 0 for the intended source-backed reason. This remains one exploratory, non-gating recurrence, not a rate or hosted review replay.

This update also preserves one measured reviewer-process proposal as an **opt-in eval-local treatment**, not as the default reviewer process. The live `.github/skills/review-pull-request/SKILL.md` remains frozen at baseline blob `b11fe9fe79b5d848687ba1c93362f4aaf22bfe53`. The treatment skill (`a8c9856cd260ad22938a2e1bfe638294abe635f3`) and reference (`f9fa346b2001a5cb551748a369c7fd78d8ca22a7`) live under `eng/skill-evals/review-pull-request/treatments/claim-validation/review-pull-request` and are selected only by `reviewer-capability-treatment.vally.yaml`.

The bounded paired comparison froze the same two projections, ordinary prompt, labels, rubric, GPT-5.6 subject, Gemini judge, Vally 0.19.0, Copilot CLI 1.0.80, Copilot SDK 1.0.15, one worker, and zero retries. Only the selected native skill/reference differed.

| Arm | Case | Run ID | Integrity | Score | Observed outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|
| baseline | #70106 | `80264656-7637-4e1d-b354-d7fbf48e22e4` | pass | 0 | A different unsupported concurrency claim targeted line 69 CTS replacement between concurrent requests and the displaced token remaining uncanceled; it was not the original line-77 event-after-check schedule. |
| baseline | #57972 | `88337c83-1a44-4be3-ac7b-51eb2869b3ff` | pass | 0 | The required `_operationTransformerContextCache` finding was missed; novel `OpenApiSchemaStore` claims remain pending manual adjudication. |
| treatment | #70106 | `2431eec9-973a-4f8f-ade6-fe399ec11a2d` | fail | 0 | The exact installed reference was read after the ledger, but the ledger included prohibited provisional reasoning and the original line-77 check-to-commit demand persisted even though the output recognized old/head equivalence. |
| treatment | #57972 | `909c0edd-0f97-490d-8ee0-4f86cbae1cb9` | pass | 0 | The phase executed, but the required positive was still missed; a novel `OpenApiSchemaStore` cache-factory claim remains pending manual adjudication. |

Accounting is closed at four reviewer CLI attempts / four actual reviewer calls and four associated-grade CLI attempts / four actual judge calls, with zero execution errors and no retries or control reruns. The authorized comparison budget is exhausted. All four semantic scores were 0, so this proposal did **not** repair the original #70106 failure, recover the required #57972 positive, or demonstrate broader reviewer improvement. Treatment #70106 also failed its own minimal-ledger process contract. Because both #57972 arms missed the required finding, the paired zeros do not demonstrate a treatment-caused recall regression. The failed candidate is retained for review rather than silently promoted or retuned.

A second opt-in proposal changed evidence/context rather than adding another same-context checklist: a claim-neutral scout emitted source citations, a deterministic gate validated the inventory, and a fresh ordinary reviewer received the validated inventory as untrusted leads. The comparison froze plan SHA-256 `8d21136fdac1953c5b09b1290a63f09ff9a188616781361b3bd7c3e0ec527dc0`, candidate-patch SHA-256 `1c4b25b6005342ca76c9152e2e12330609d132ea3af66cdc6581551d5bc57088`, and tree `783d4564e9e27b95647d0b4ddf5b3f614a828b1e`; commit `897fa4efabf3ed9388233d19b320cf4dc876d990` published that exact tree before execution. Treatment used two reviewer executions per case versus one baseline execution and added inventory/native-delta/forced-complete-view constraints, so attribution is limited to this evidence-augmentation pipeline. The pinned npm/platform package was `1.0.80`, while the exact shared binary reported `1.0.105` and hashed `4f590f1f60f3f2bd4cf731cddf50360672d3c97d93150bd05ffa496d65e326f8`.

| Stage | Case | Run ID | Integrity | Score | Observed outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---:|---|
| baseline | #70106 | `d7baf99f-23e1-4526-bee6-caccb66630bf` | pass | 0 | Reported a distinct line-69 CTS-replacement candidate. The grade marked it `MANUAL_ADJUDICATION_REQUIRED`; it remains pending, not a source-proven recurrence of the original line-77 mechanism. |
| baseline | #57972 | `bd427ddc-78ed-4df7-810c-31d8b52f26a3` | pass | 0 | Missed required `_operationTransformerContextCache`; two `OpenApiSchemaStore` claims remain pending manual adjudication. |
| scout | #70106 | `5500d779-3b38-419d-9efb-b5050179d670` | pass | N/A | Produced a valid 27-item, four-file projected inventory. |
| finalizer | #70106 | `52d41550-8ee2-493e-a780-8a17f6f1b204` | fail | 1 | Returned `NO_FINDINGS` and received judge score 1, but `required/pull/body.source` was read at event 79 after the installed reference at event 44 and inventory at event 45, violating the frozen core-before-reference-before-inventory protocol. The score is the saved semantic outcome, not proof of latent understanding. |
| scout | #57972 | `bde60a8f-e65d-4949-a3b4-80e4ec0008e0` | fail | N/A | Returned six coverage rows with no evidence links and only two duplicate pull-scope entries. `E001-C01` copied the body excerpt but supplied the raw-file hash rather than the required LF-joined excerpt hash. |
| finalizer | #57972 | `64632659-10ab-4e83-9c9d-bc453be8be4e` | not run | N/A | The failed scout stopped only its dependent finalizer and grade; neither has a score. |

The paid phase closed at five reviewer executions and three grades, with zero retries, controls, variants, or platform execution errors. Three authorized reviewer slots remained unused: the dependency-skipped #57972 finalizer plus the two slots reserved as unavailable rather than retry capacity. Both treatment cases failed required mechanism Integrity, so this proposal is not a demonstrated repair and remains opt-in/default-disabled. The #70106 protocol failure does not prove evidence scouting can never help; the unexecuted #57972 finalizer provides no treatment recall result.

Issues.Title: Avoid StringBuilder when encoding Content-Disposition file names
Issues.Body:
`ContentDispositionHeaderValue.SetHttpFileName` runs for every file result with a download name (`Results.File(..., fileDownloadName: ...)`, MVC `FileResult`, via `FileResultHelper`). It always computes `filename*` with `Encode5987`. That method built the value with a `StringBuilder`, appending each percent-encoded byte through an interpolated-string append. Quoting a non-token `filename` also went through `string.Format(CultureInfo.InvariantCulture, "\"{0}\"", segment)`, which boxes the `StringSegment`.

## Changes
- `Encode5987`: compute the exact output length first. Each non-attr-char rune adds `Utf8SequenceLength * 3`, and invalid surrogates count as U+FFFD, matching `Rune.DecodeFromUtf16`. Then:
  - if nothing needs encoding, return `string.Concat("UTF-8''", value)`;
  - otherwise, write the string once with `string.Create`.
- The UTF-8 bit math in `EncodeToUtf8Hex` is unchanged; it now writes `%XX` directly into the destination span.
- `EncodeAndQuoteMime`: `string.Concat("\"", value, "\"")` replaces `string.Format`.

The output is identical. New tests assert the full header string for:
- ASCII, spaces, and quote/backslash escaping;
- 2-, 3- and 4-byte UTF-8;
- lone high and low surrogates.

They pass on `main` and on this branch. The existing `FileNameStar_WhenNeedsEncoding_UsesHex` covers every ASCII byte.

Issues.Title: Reuse a cached StringBuilder when formatting header values
Issues.Body:
Formatting typed header values (`CacheControlHeaderValue`, `MediaTypeHeaderValue`, `ContentDispositionHeaderValue`, `ContentRangeHeaderValue`, `RangeHeaderValue`, `NameValueHeaderValue.ToString(list)`) allocated a fresh `StringBuilder` per call. These run on common response paths: `ResponseHeaders.CacheControl`/`ContentDisposition`/`ContentRange` setters, file results with range processing, and OutputCaching/ResponseCaching.

## Changes
- Add an internal `StringBuilderCache` (one `[ThreadStatic]` builder per thread, reused only when capacity ≤ 360 chars). The builder never leaves the formatting method. Only the resulting `string` is returned, and the builder is cleared on acquire, so nothing cached is reachable by callers or shared between requests. A nested acquire just gets a new builder.
- `ContentDispositionHeaderValue.ToString` builds into a single builder instead of concatenating `_dispositionType` with a separately built parameter string.
- Integer formatting in `CacheControlHeaderValue`/`ContentRangeHeaderValue` uses `Append(NumberFormatInfo.InvariantInfo, $"...")` instead of an intermediate `ToString(InvariantInfo)` string. Output is still invariant.

No public API or output changes. The new `HeaderValueToStringTest` covers:
- sequential reuse with no stale content;
- values longer than the cache limit;
- the exact ContentDisposition output;
- invariant numbers under a culture with a custom `NegativeSign`.

Issues.Title: Validate newline chars in HTTP/3 dynamic-table header values
Issues.Body:
### Summary

`Http3Stream.OnHeaderCore` passes `checkForNewlineChars: false` for a `HeaderType.Dynamic` header resolved by name, while the identical switch case in `Http2Connection.OnHeaderCore` passes `true`. This PR makes the HTTP/3 side match.

#68743 (which closed #68371) made exactly two source changes:

| file | change |
| --- | --- |
| `Http2Connection.cs`, `case HeaderType.Dynamic` | `checkForNewlineChars: false` -> `true` |
| `HttpProtocol.cs`, `OnTrailer` | `checkForNewlineChars: false` -> `true` |

`HttpProtocol.OnTrailer` is protocol-agnostic, which is why the HTTP/3 trailer tests added in that PR pass without any HTTP/3 source change. The HTTP/3 counterpart of the *first* change was not made.

### Is this reachable today?

No, and this PR does not claim otherwise.

`HPackDecoder` is the only caller of `OnDynamicIndexedHeader` in the product (`src/Shared/runtime/Http2/Hpack/HPackDecoder.cs`), and it is HTTP/2 only. `QPackDecoder` invokes just three callbacks, all of which land on paths that already validate:

- `OnStaticIndexedHeader(index, value)` -> `TryQPackAppend(index, value, checkForNewlineChars: !indexOnly)`
- `OnHeader(name, value)` -> `ValidateHeaderContent` plus `checkForNewlineChars: true`
- `OnStaticIndexedHeader(index)` -> static-table value

Kestrel does not implement the QPACK dynamic table, so this branch cannot be reached from the network.

### Why change it anyway

The two switch statements are otherwise identical, and within the HTTP/3 switch the neighbouring `HeaderType.NameAndValue` case validates while this one does not, with no comment explaining the difference. Setting it to `true` now means the line is correct by construction if the QPACK dynamic table (RFC 9204 section 3.2) is ever implemented, rather than shipping on day one with the HTTP/2 bug that #68743 fixed.

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [ ] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable. No test is added: the branch cannot be exercised through the decoder, and the HTTP/2 analogue is covered by `OnDynamicIndexedHeader_NewlineCharactersInValue_ThrowsConnectionError`, which calls the handler directly. The server-side `Http3Stream` is not exposed by the in-memory HTTP/3 test harness, which hands tests the client-side `Http3RequestStream`. Happy to add one behind a test hook if you would prefer that.
- [ ] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable. Not applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. The related issue is #68371, closed by #68743. I did not open a new one because nothing is reachable here, but happy to if you prefer.

Issues.Title: Reduce allocations in QueryHelpers.AddQueryString
Issues.Body:
`QueryHelpers.AddQueryString` builds its result with a default-capacity `StringBuilder`, which grows chunk by chunk. The single name/value overload also wraps the pair in an array and goes through `IEnumerable` enumeration. The single-pair overload runs on hot paths such as cookie authentication login/access-denied redirects (`ReturnUrl`), and the dictionary overload runs when building OAuth/OIDC challenge URLs.

Changes (all internal to `QueryHelpers`, no public API change):
- **`AddQueryString(string uri, string name, string value)`:** computes the encoded name and value, then builds the result in one `string.Create`. Base URI, then `?` or `&` (decided exactly as before: is there a `?` before the first `#`), then `name=value`, then the anchor.
- **Enumerable overloads:** append into a private `ArrayPool<char>`-backed buffer instead of `StringBuilder`, then copy into a fresh string. The rented buffer never leaves the method and is returned in `finally`.

The output is identical: same separators, same `UrlEncoder.Default` encoding, `null` values skipped, anchor preserved.

### Benchmark
`QueryHelpersAddQueryStringBenchmark` (added): BenchmarkDotNet InProcess, 3 interleaved main/PR rounds:

| Case | main | PR | main alloc | PR alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `ReturnUrl` (single pair, value needs encoding) | 156.2 / 152.5 / 150.4 ns | 86.5 / 87.9 / 88.6 ns (−43%) | 600 B | 216 B (−64%) |
| `Simple` (single pair, no encoding) | 66.4 / 67.2 / 68.8 ns | 26.3 / 28.0 / 26.1 ns (−60%) | 304 B | 56 B (−82%) |
| `OAuth` (7-entry dictionary) | 503.9 / 508.9 / 492.4 ns | 410.7 / 367.7 / 373.7 ns (−24%) | 2,072 B | 952 B (−54%) |

### Tests
Added `AddQueryStringMatchesReferenceImplementation`, which compares both the single-pair and the enumerable overloads against the previous `StringBuilder` algorithm. Cases cover empty URIs, a trailing `?`, `#` inside the anchor and multiple `#`, a `?` inside the fragment, non-ASCII and surrogate pairs, characters that need encoding, `null` values, and 1,400-char keys and values (longer once encoded) that force the pooled buffer to grow. A mutation that drops the copy in the growth path fails 8 of these cases. All 514 WebUtilities tests pass.

# Avoid per-request policy list, enumerator and tag set allocations in OutputCacheMiddleware

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making.

Removes 3-4 allocations from every request that output caching handles.

## Description
For each request with an output cache policy, `OutputCacheMiddleware`:
- builds the policy list in `TryGetRequestPolicies` as a `List<IOutputCachePolicy>`. That is a list object plus a backing array that grows on `Add`.
- iterates it with `foreach` over `IReadOnlyList<IOutputCachePolicy>`. Each loop boxes a `List<T>.Enumerator`, and there are 2 loops per request: `CacheRequestAsync` plus either `ServeFromCacheAsync` (hit) or `ServeResponseAsync` (miss).

This change:
- counts the policies first and allocates a single array of the exact size. The order is unchanged: base policies, then endpoint `IOutputCachePolicy` metadata, then `[OutputCache]` attribute.
- replaces the three `foreach` loops over the interface with indexed `for` loops.
- creates `OutputCacheContext.Tags` on first access instead of in the constructor. Only `TagsPolicy` and the store path use it, so requests without tag policies no longer allocate an empty `HashSet<string>`. The public `Tags` getter keeps the same shape and semantics: it is never null and returns the same instance on every access.

The list was private to the request and never exposed. There are no behavior, cache key, stored format or header changes, and no public API changes.

Benchmark: new `MiddlewareBenchmarks.CacheHit`. It runs the full middleware with `MemoryOutputCacheStore` and serves a cache hit, including the `DefaultHttpContext` creation. Three interleaved A/B rounds:

| BasePolicy | Before (main) | After |
|---|---|---|
| false (endpoint policy only, no tags) | 1.817-1.879 us / 3,720 B | 1.744-1.792 us / 3,520 B |
| true (base policy with a tag + endpoint policy) | 1.947-2.029 us / 3,832 B | 1.829-1.936 us / 3,704 B |

This is an allocation win: 200 B fewer per request without tags and 128 B with tags (the set is still needed then). Time improves by about 3-5%, which is close to noise. Byte counts come from runs with `SizeUnit.B`; the repo's default summary rounds to KB.

Tests: Microsoft.AspNetCore.OutputCaching.Tests, 415/415. New tests check how `TryGetRequestPolicies` combines base, endpoint and attribute policies and their order, that policy tags (0, 1 or 2) still reach `IOutputCacheStore.SetAsync`, and that `Tags` returns a stable instance. They also pass against main.

`ShouldCompressResponse` no longer allocates strings to match the response Content-Type.

## Description
`ResponseCompressionProvider.ShouldCompressResponse` runs on the first write of every response that goes through the middleware. On main it allocates:
- `Substring` + `Trim` when the Content-Type has parameters. This is the common case, e.g. `application/json; charset=utf-8` or `text/html; charset=utf-8`; 56 B.
- `string.Concat(type, "/*")` for the partial `type/*` lookup whenever the exact type isn't configured, e.g. `image/png`; 40 B.

Changes (all internal/private):
- When the Content-Type has no parameters, the exact lookup still uses the `string`, so that path isn't slowed down. When it has parameters, the trimmed media type is looked up as a `ReadOnlySpan<char>` through `HashSet<string>.GetAlternateLookup` (same `OrdinalIgnoreCase` comparer).
- The partial match uses two sets built once in the constructor. They hold the `type` part of the configured `type/*` entries, one set for included and one for excluded entries. The lookup gives the same result as `ShouldCompressExact("type/*")` without building that string. Excluded entries are still checked before included ones.
- The "not enabled for Content-Type" Debug log only materializes the media-type string when Debug logging is enabled. The logged value is unchanged.

Behavior, options handling, log messages and headers are unchanged.

|---|---|---|
| `application/json; charset=utf-8` | 85.8-88.8 ns / 56 B | 74.8-79.0 ns / 0 B |
| `image/png` (not compressible, partial lookup) | 102.0-105.1 ns / 40 B | 80.7-82.2 ns / 0 B |
| `text/html` | 69.1-71.0 ns / 0 B | 69.6-71.9 ns / 0 B |

Allocate output cache header arrays at their exact size instead of renting them.

## Description
`OutputCacheEntryFormatter.Deserialize` (every cache hit) and `OutputCacheEntry.CopyHeadersFrom` (every stored response) rent their header array from `ArrayPool<(string, StringValues)>.Shared`, but the arrays are never returned: `OutputCacheEntry.Dispose` is a no-op, and the entry keeps the array. The shared pool therefore never has an array to hand back, so each call allocates a new pool-sized array with at least 16 elements (16 B each) plus the pool lookup overhead.

This change allocates an array of exactly the needed length. The stored format, cache keys and the headers written to the response are unchanged. Because nothing is rented, no array can be shared between entries.

| 10 | 154-170 ns / 488 B | 136-143 ns / 328 B |

| 65553 | 151-162 ns / 488 B | 138-139 ns / 328 B |
| 262161 | 149-158 ns / 488 B | 137-142 ns / 328 B |

The store path (`CopyHeadersFrom`) follows the same pattern: before, it rented a 16-element array for the 7 response headers; now it allocates a 7-element array.

Issues.Title: Write AES-GCM key modifier and nonce directly into the output buffer
Issues.Body:
Write AES-GCM key modifier and nonce directly into the output buffer

## Description

`AesGcmAuthenticatedEncryptor.Encrypt` allocated two small arrays per call, `GenRandom(16)` for the key modifier and `GenRandom(12)` for the nonce, then copied them into the output buffer. The span overload `IManagedGenRandom.GenRandom(Span<byte>)` (backed by `RandomNumberGenerator.Fill`) now writes them directly into their final positions in the output buffer. The derived-key context reads the key modifier from that same slice. The RNG calls happen in the same order with the same sizes.

Issues.Title: Build the DataProtection AAD template lazily

Build the DataProtection AAD template lazily

## Description

Every `KeyRingBasedDataProtector` built its additional authenticated data (AAD) template (`magic || keyId || purposeCount || purposes…`, UTF-8 encoded) in its constructor. In a purpose chain such as `provider.CreateProtector("Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.Cookies.CookieAuthenticationMiddleware", "Cookies", "v2")`, plus the application discriminator that `AddDataProtection` adds, every intermediate protector built and encoded a template for its prefix of the chain. That is O(n²) UTF-8 work, but only the leaf protector ever protects or unprotects.

The template is now built on the first `Protect`/`Unprotect` (`GetAadForKey`) and published with `Interlocked.CompareExchange`. The cache works as before: the template is cached per protector instance and updated for the default key on protect. To keep `CreateProtector` behavior unchanged, the constructor still eagerly validates the newly added purpose with the same `SecureUtf8Encoding.GetByteCount`. An invalid purpose, such as a lone surrogate, still throws `EncoderFallbackException` from `CreateProtector`. Earlier purposes in the chain were already validated when their protectors were created (the only constructor callers are `KeyRingBasedDataProtectionProvider.CreateProtector` with no prior purposes, and `KeyRingBasedDataProtector.CreateProtector` with its own validated `Purposes`).

Found by profiling (EventPipe allocation sampling): `BuildAadTemplateBytes` accounted for about 60% of allocations in `CreateProtector` chains.

### Benchmarks
Linux x64, 2 cores, BenchmarkDotNet in-process, 3 interleaved rounds vs main (median). Provider from `AddDataProtection` (includes the app discriminator), default algorithms.

| Scenario | main | PR | main alloc | PR alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CreateProtector(cookie chain)` only | 0.47 us | 0.19 us (-59%) | 776 B | 344 B (-56%) |
| `CreateProtector(cookie chain)` + Protect 100 B | 10.59 us | 10.57 us | 2,296 B | 2,024 B (-12%) |
| `CreateProtector(antiforgery, single purpose)` + Protect 100 B | 10.14 us | 10.05 us | 1,672 B | 1,680 B (+8 B) |

The single-purpose case has no intermediate protectors to save. It pays 8 bytes for the extra reference kept in the template struct.

### Security reasoning
- **AAD bytes unchanged:** the same `BuildAadTemplateBytes` builds the template from the same purposes, and the key id is written exactly as before. A new test checks that the lazily built AAD equals the eagerly built template. Existing tests cover byte-level compatibility of `BuildAadTemplateBytes` (`ReturnsSameResultAsPreviousImplementation`) and protect/unprotect round-trips.
- **No sharing across purposes:** the template remains private state of a single protector instance and is derived only from that protector's own purposes. Nothing is shared between protectors or reachable by callers.
- **Thread safety:** the first build is published with `Interlocked.CompareExchange`, so concurrent first callers agree on one immutable template (new concurrency test). The existing `Volatile` read/write logic for key changes is unchanged.
- **Exceptions unchanged:** invalid purposes still throw from `CreateProtector` (new test). No public API change, no PublicAPI.*.txt changes, no unsafe code added. No crypto, comparison or validation logic is touched, and the key ring is still not resolved by `CreateProtector`.

Issues.Body:
Avoid intermediate copies in TimeLimitedDataProtector

## Description

`TimeLimitedDataProtector.Protect` copied the plaintext into a new `{ expiration (8 B, big-endian UTC ticks) || plaintext }` array before protecting it, and `Unprotect` received the full `{ expiration || plaintext }` array from the inner protector and then copied the payload into a second array.

On .NET, when the inner protector implements `ISpanDataProtector` (which `CreateProtector` always returns on .NET), it now:
- **Protect:** writes the header and plaintext into an `ArrayPool<byte>` buffer (returned with `clearArray: true`) and protects it into a pooled writer (cleared on grow and dispose). The only array allocated is the returned protected payload.
- **Unprotect:** unprotects into the pooled, clearing writer, validates the header and expiration exactly as before, and copies only the payload into the returned array.

The header format, the expiration check, the error messages and the exception homogenization (`try`/`catch` → `CryptographicException`) are unchanged. Non-span inner protectors and non-.NET TFMs use the existing code.

Found by profiling (EventPipe CPU + allocation sampling): the header+plaintext copies were 28–46% of the allocations in the TimeLimited scenarios.

### Benchmarks
Linux x64, 2 cores, BenchmarkDotNet in-process, 3 interleaved rounds vs main (median). `ToTimeLimitedDataProtector()` over a cookie-style purpose chain, 2 KB payload.

| Alg | Scenario | main | PR | main alloc | PR alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| CBC | Protect 2 KB | 14.21 us | 13.82 us | 7,328 B | 2,912 B (-60%) |
| CBC | Unprotect 2 KB | 9.78 us | 9.57 us | 4,704 B | 2,624 B (-44%) |
| GCM | Protect 2 KB | 8.65 us | 8.67 us | 4,576 B | 2,496 B (-45%) |
| GCM | Unprotect 2 KB | 6.41 us | 6.24 us | 4,424 B | 2,344 B (-47%) |

Time is neutral (within noise); the win is allocation.

### Custom (byte[]-only) encryptors
All built-in encryptors (managed CBC/GCM, CNG CBC/GCM) implement `ISpanAuthenticatedEncryptor` and take the zero-copy path above. For a custom byte[]-only `IAuthenticatedEncryptor`, `KeyRingBasedSpanDataProtector` falls back to copying the ciphertext span. ca43838480 removes the avoidable AAD copy in that fallback. Measured with a byte[]-only wrapper around the managed CBC encryptor, 2 KB payload: Protect 8,297 B → 8,224 B (neutral); Unprotect 5,818 B → 7,780 B (one ciphertext-sized copy). The trade-off is discussed in the review thread.

### Security reasoning
- **Byte-identical payloads:** the inner protector gets exactly the same bytes as before. The new known-answer theory `Protect_SpanInnerProtector_ProducesSamePayloadAsByteArrayPath` (0 B–70 KB) uses a real `KeyRingBasedSpanDataProtector` with a deterministic RNG. It asserts the span path output equals the existing byte[] path output (the inner protector is wrapped to hide `ISpanDataProtector`), and that each path unprotects the other's payload with the same expiration.
- **Plaintext hygiene improves:** both pooled buffers hold plaintext and are zeroed before being returned to the pool. Previously the intermediate `{ expiration || plaintext }` arrays were left to the GC without being zeroed. No key material passes through these buffers.
- **Nothing pooled is caller-reachable:** the buffers are scoped to one call; only freshly allocated result arrays escape.
- **Exceptions unchanged:** the span path runs inside the same homogenizing `try`, with the same "payload invalid" and "payload expired" errors (covered by new tests). No public API change, no PublicAPI.*.txt changes, no unsafe code. No crypto, comparison or validation logic is touched.

### Overlap
No overlap with #70146 (managed encryptor internals). This PR adds the same internal `ClearingPooledBufferWriter` (shared source, `src/DataProtection/shared/src`) as #70187; the file is byte-identical, so whichever merges second has no conflict.

Issues.Title: Avoid parsing the Accept header on non-SSE SignalR connection GETs
Issues.Body:
`HttpConnectionDispatcher.ExecuteAsync` handles every GET to a connection endpoint, which includes each long-polling poll and each WebSocket upgrade. On every one of those GETs it called `GetTypedHeaders().Accept`, which parses the whole `Accept` header into `MediaTypeHeaderValue`s, just to check for `text/event-stream`.

## Change
The new `IsServerSentEventsRequest` first scans the raw `Accept` values for the substring `event-stream` (OrdinalIgnoreCase). It runs the **original** typed-header check only when that substring is present.

A parsed media type that equals `text/event-stream` requires the raw header to contain the contiguous ASCII token `event-stream`. So the prefilter can only produce false positives, and those fall through to the unchanged original check. Behavior is identical. There are no public API or wire changes.

## Results
Side-by-side BenchmarkDotNet run on a `DefaultHttpContext`, 3 rounds (TypedParse is the current code, Prefilter is this PR):

| Accept | Before | After | Alloc |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| (none) | 43–48 ns | 5.2 ns | 48 B → 0 |
| `*/*` | 132–138 ns | 12.2–12.8 ns | 184 B → 0 |
| browser default (`text/html,...,*/*;q=0.8`) | 754–767 ns | 22.1–22.2 ns | 864 B → 0 |
| `text/event-stream` (once per SSE connection) | 144.5 ns | 178–198 ns | 184 → 208 B |

Hot GET paths, meaning every long-poll and every WebSocket upgrade, are 8–34× faster and allocation-free. The SSE GET happens only once per connection and costs about 40 ns more.

## Description

`DataProtectionCommonExtensions.Protect(string)` / `Unprotect(string)` (used by TempData, antiforgery-style consumers, and many apps) allocated a UTF-8 `byte[]` of the plaintext, then the protected `byte[]`, then the Base64Url string (and the reverse for `Unprotect`). - protect/unprotect into a new internal `ClearingPooledBufferWriter` (pooled; the array is cleared every time it grows and on dispose),

# Fast path for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 :path validation

- [x] You've read the Contributor Guide and Code of Conduct.
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (Perf-only change, no issue.)

Skip narrowing `:path` to bytes and running `PathDecoder` for the common clean paths in HTTP/2 and HTTP/3.

## Description

For every request, `Http2Stream.TryValidatePath` and `Http3Stream.TryValidatePath` copy the `:path` chars into a byte buffer one char at a time. They then call `PathDecoder.DecodePath`, which scans for dot segments and either returns `RawTarget` or creates an ASCII string from the bytes.

Most request paths have no `%` and no `/.`. For those paths, `DecodePath` returns one of two values:
- If there's no query, it returns `RawTarget`. Each char must still be `<= 0xFF`; the narrowing loop already enforces that.
- If there's a query, it returns `GetAsciiString(path)`. That call throws for non-ASCII input, and the stream is then reset.

The new fast path returns the same results directly. `ContainsAnyExceptInRange(0, 0xFF)` covers the case with no query, and `Ascii.IsValid` plus `ToString()` covers the case with a query. Any input outside these cases falls through to the existing code, which is unchanged. That includes percent-encoded paths, dot segments and anything the old code would reject. Rejection behavior and error messages therefore stay the same.

This adds no new unsafe code, no new stackalloc and no API changes.

### Benchmark

This PR adds `Http2StreamHeadersBenchmark`. It drives a pooled `Http2Stream` through Reset, the `OnHeader` callbacks for a typical 8-header browser GET, `OnHeadersComplete` and `TryParseRequest`. The table shows results from BenchmarkDotNet (short job) over three interleaved A/B rounds:

# Materialize trimmed [Authorize] roles once in AuthorizationPolicy.CombineAsync

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. (Perf finding from end-to-end profiling, no separate issue.)

Stop re-trimming `[Authorize(Roles = ...)]` role names on every request.

## Description

### Motivation (found by end-to-end profiling)
I profiled an end-to-end authorization pipeline: a per-request DI scope, `DefaultHttpContext`, `AuthorizationMiddleware`, and an endpoint with `[Authorize]`, `[Authorize("Policy")]`, `[Authorize(Roles = "...")]` and `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]`. The trace was collected with dotnet-trace using AllocationTick and showed an `ArrayWhereSelectIterator<string, string>` allocated on **every request**. It accounted for about 7% of the allocated bytes.

`AuthorizationPolicy.CombineAsync` turns `AuthorizeAttribute.Roles` into the following:

```csharp
var trimmedRolesSplit = rolesSplit.Where(r => !string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(r)).Select(r => r.Trim());
policyBuilder.RequireRole(trimmedRolesSplit);
```

`RolesAuthorizationRequirement` stores that **lazy** query as `AllowedRoles`. The combined policy is then cached per endpoint by `AuthorizationPolicyCache` in `AuthorizationMiddleware`, and by MVC's `AuthorizeFilter`. As a result, every authorization check re-runs the query. Each re-run does three things:
- It allocates the `Where/Select` iterator.
- It re-runs `IsNullOrWhiteSpace`.
- It calls `Trim()` again on each role it reaches. For the common `Roles = "Admin, Manager"` style, that allocates a new string per role on every request.

### Change
- `CombineAsync` now materializes the trimmed, non-empty roles into a `string[]` once, when the policy is built. The roles and their order are unchanged. Whitespace-only entries are still skipped, and an all-whitespace `Roles` still throws the same `InvalidOperationException` from the `RolesAuthorizationRequirement` ctor.
- `RolesAuthorizationRequirement.HandleRequirementAsync` iterates `string[]` directly, which is the shape produced both by `CombineAsync` and by `RequireRole(params string[])`. It falls back to the existing `IEnumerable<string>` loop for any other collection, so user-supplied collections are still enumerated live, exactly as before.

There are no public API changes. `AllowedRoles` is still `IEnumerable<string>` with the same contents.

### Security reasoning
- The same roles are checked with the same `ClaimsPrincipal.IsInRole` semantics, in the same order and with the same short-circuiting.
- Nothing derived from the user or principal is cached. The only thing computed once is the role list from the static `[Authorize]` metadata, which was already captured in the cached policy.
- No pooling, no crypto, and no wire-format involvement.

### Benchmarks
The harness is a local BenchmarkDotNet end-to-end run, in-process, with 5 warmup and 15 measured iterations. Each request creates a DI scope and a `DefaultHttpContext` and runs `AuthorizationMiddleware` with the cached policy. Allocated bytes per request were measured exactly with `GC.GetTotalAllocatedBytes` over 20k requests.

**Authorization only** (`[Authorize]`, `[Authorize("AdminPolicy")]`, `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin,User")]`, `[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]`), 3 A/B rounds:

| Round | main Mean ± Error | PR Mean ± Error | Δ time |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.601 µs ± 0.024 | 2.455 µs ± 0.020 | −5.6% |
| 2 | 2.661 µs ± 0.022 | 2.451 µs ± 0.016 | −7.9% |
| 3 | 2.694 µs ± 0.017 | 2.489 µs ± 0.028 | −7.6% |

| Scenario (allocated per request) | main | PR | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Roles = `"Admin,User"` (no spaces) | 4,848 B | 4,416 B | **−432 B (−8.9%)** |
| Roles = `"Manager, Editor, Admin"` (spaces, user matches last role) | 5,304 B | 4,656 B | **−648 B (−12.2%)** |

**Full cookie-authenticated request** (`AuthenticationMiddleware`, then the cookie handler, DataProtection Unprotect, `AuthorizationMiddleware` with a policy plus `Roles = "Admin,User"`):

| Round | main Mean ± Error | PR Mean ± Error |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 11.97 µs ± 0.100 | 11.88 µs ± 0.087 |
| 2 | 12.10 µs ± 0.145 | 11.94 µs ± 0.126 |
| 3 | 12.15 µs ± 0.075 | 11.98 µs ± 0.157 |

Allocations went from 13,344 B to 13,168 B per request (−176 B). Time is within noise and no worse, because DataProtection dominates this path.

### Tests
- New `AuthorizationPolicyFacts.CombineTrimsRolesOnceAndPreservesOrder` checks the order and trimming, and that repeated enumeration returns the same string instances. It fails on main.
- New `AuthorizationPolicyFacts.CombineThrowsForRolesWithOnlyWhitespaceEntries` pins the existing exception behavior.
- New `DefaultAuthorizationServiceTests.RolePolicyWithNonArrayRolesCanRequireOneOfManyRoles` covers the non-array fallback path.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authorization.Test`: 172/172 passed.
- `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Mvc.Core.Test` filtered to `Authoriz`, which includes the `AuthorizeFilter` tests: 85/85 passed.

## Description

`ContentDispositionHeaderValue.Name` / `FileName` call `TryDecodeMime` on every get. For any quoted value of 10+ characters (e.g. `name="attachment"`) it ran `Split('?').ToArray()`, which allocates a boxed enumerator, a list and an array, even though the value is almost never MIME-encoded. `FormFeature` and `MultipartReader` sections call these getters 3–4 times per section (`IsFileDisposition`, `IsFormDisposition`, `Name`, `FileName`).

This replaces the split with a span-based shape check: a `"=?` prefix, a `?="` suffix and exactly two inner `?`. It accepts exactly the same inputs as `parts.Length == 5 && parts[0] == "\"=" && parts[4] == "=\""`. The decode path (`Encoding.GetEncoding`, `Convert.FromBase64String`) is unchanged. No public API or behavior change.

### Benchmark

New `ContentDispositionParseBenchmarks` (TryParse + `IsFileDisposition`/`IsFormDisposition` + `Name`/`FileName`, mirroring `FormFeature`). InProcess, 3 interleaved rounds:

| 2 | 269.0 ns / 408 B | 200.8 ns / 264 B | 473.6 ns / 888 B | 337.3 ns / 456 B |
| 3 | 251.2 ns / 408 B | 207.7 ns / 264 B | 483.5 ns / 888 B | 339.1 ns / 456 B |

# Pre-size the HttpLogging parameter lists

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [ ] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

Removes the intermediate array growth when `HttpLoggingMiddleware` collects request and response parameters.

## Description

For each logged request, `HttpLoggingMiddleware` adds the request properties and every request header to `HttpLoggingInterceptorContext.InternalParameters`, and later adds the status code and every response header. That list can't be pooled because the `HttpLog` state may be kept by a logger. Every request starts with an empty list, so it grows 0 → 4 → 8 → 16 (→ 32) and throws away each intermediate `KeyValuePair<string, object?>[]`.

Before adding parameters, the list is now sized **exactly** (`Capacity = Count + n`), with `n` counted from the enabled fields only:
- **Request** (in `InvokeInternal`): Protocol, Method and Scheme add 1 each, RequestPath adds 2 (PathBase and Path), RequestQuery adds 1, plus `Headers.Count` when RequestHeaders is enabled. With `CombineLogs`, the known response slots (status code, bodies, duration) are reserved here too.
- **Response** (in `LogResponseHeadersCore`, the shared path used by the middleware, `ResponseBufferingStream` and `UpgradeFeatureLoggingDecorator`): StatusCode adds 1, plus `Headers.Count` when ResponseHeaders is enabled. Duration and body slots are counted only for combined logs.

`Count` already includes any parameters interceptors added. When nothing is enabled, nothing is reserved. Only the list's capacity changes. Its contents, order, log output and the `Parameters` view seen by interceptors are identical. No public API changes.

## Benchmark

Local BenchmarkDotNet, 3 runs each, net12.0, 2 cores. The pipeline is `AddHttpLogging` + `UseHttpLogging`, with default fields unless noted. The logger is enabled and calls the formatter, like a console sink. Each op is a new `DefaultHttpContext` with 9 request headers; the endpoint sets 3 response headers. `ContextOnly` (context creation alone) is ~470 ns, 2016 B in both.

| Case | main Mean (3 runs) | PR Mean (3 runs) | main Alloc | PR Alloc |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DefaultFields | 1545 / 1549 / 1597 ns (±18–32) | 1480 / 1487 / 1467 ns (±10–27) | 4080 B | **3808 B (−272 B)** |
| CombineLogs | 1495 / 1521 / 1482 ns (±24–27) | 1411 / 1468 / 1437 ns (±25–29) | 4432 B | **3952 B (−480 B)** |
| CombineLogs + Duration + Query | 1651 / 1626 / 1679 ns (±22–33) | 1584 / 1658 / 1624 ns (±23–27) | 4568 B | **4152 B (−416 B)** |
| DefaultFields + Duration | 1713 / 1759 / 1731 ns (±9–31) | 1617 / 1675 / 1714 ns (±13–33) | 4143 B | **3872 B (−271 B)** |
| RequestMethod only | 823 / 797 / 808 ns (±9–15) | 808 / 811 / 795 ns (±14–16) | 2488 B | **2440 B (−48 B)** |

The middleware's own allocation drops 13–20% (for example 2064 → 1792 B for DefaultFields and 2416 → 1936 B for CombineLogs). Time improves 2–5%. The savings grow with header count.

# Skip the endpoint rate limiter when the endpoint has no rate limiting policy

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

Removes redundant per-request work in `RateLimitingMiddleware` when only a `GlobalLimiter` applies.

## Description

With a `GlobalLimiter` configured, every request to an endpoint **without** `[EnableRateLimiting]` (or `RequireRateLimiting`) still goes through the endpoint `PartitionedRateLimiter`. Its partitioner reads the endpoint metadata again, finds no attribute and returns `RateLimitPartition.GetNoLimiter(_defaultPolicyKey)`. The `DefaultPartitionedRateLimiter` then looks up that partition (lock plus dictionary lookup) and returns the shared `NoopLimiter` lease. The middleware then allocates a `DefaultCombinedLease(globalLease, noopLease)`.

`InvokeInternal` already knows whether the endpoint has an `EnableRateLimitingAttribute`. When it doesn't, `CombinedAcquire` / `CombinedWaitAsync` now return the global lease directly.

This is equivalent because:
- With no attribute, the endpoint partitioner always returns the no-op partition.
- `NoopLimiter.AttemptAcquire/AcquireAsync` always succeed, ignore cancellation, and return a static lease with no metadata.
- An acquired lease is only disposed by the middleware; it never reaches user code (only rejected leases are passed to `OnRejected`).

Global-rejection, endpoint-rejection, queuing, cancellation and metrics paths are unchanged. On the queued path, the skipped no-op `AcquireAsync` would have observed an already-canceled `RequestAborted`, so the skip branch calls `ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` to keep that behavior. Endpoints with a policy take exactly the same path as before. No public API changes.

## Benchmark

Local BenchmarkDotNet, 3 runs each, net12.0, 2 cores. The pipeline is built with `AddRateLimiter` + `UseRateLimiter`. Each op is `new DefaultHttpContext()` with an endpoint set (`ContextOnly` ≈ 175 ns, 1048 B). Limiters are `ConcurrencyLimiter`s with large permit limits.

| Global limiter, endpoint with policy | 574 / 614 / 559 ns | 564 / 571 / 562 ns | — | 1408 B | 1408 B |
| Endpoint policy only | 442 / 458 / 461 ns | 450 / 465 / 455 ns | — | 1216 B | 1216 B |

## Tests

  - `GlobalOnly_NoEndpointPolicy_RequestAbortedWhileQueued_ReleasesGlobalLeaseAndSkipsNext`: the global lease is granted while the request is being aborted. It is released, `next` is skipped and "The request was canceled." is logged, matching main.

`StatusCodePagesMiddleware` allocates `HttpContext.Items` on every request, even when nothing uses it.

## Description

#62178 added `context.Items[nameof(StatusCodePagesOptions)] = _options.PathFormat` before `next` and `Items.Remove(...)` after it, so Blazor's `EndpointHtmlRenderer` can find the re-execute path (`Items[...] as string`).

With `UseStatusCodePages()` or `UseStatusCodePagesWithRedirects(...)`, `PathFormat` is `null`. Writing that `null` still forces `DefaultHttpContext` to create its `ItemsFeature`, the `ItemsDictionary` and the inner `Dictionary<object, object?>` on **every request**, even when nothing else in the pipeline uses `Items`.

Reading `Items[key]` returns `null` for a missing key, the same as for a stored `null`. So when `PathFormat` is null **and** the request's `Items` has not been created yet (the context is exactly `DefaultHttpContext` and `IItemsFeature` is null), the write is skipped.

> [!NOTE]
> **One observable difference (raised in review):** when `PathFormat` is null and `Items` is first materialized *downstream*, `Items.ContainsKey(nameof(StatusCodePagesOptions))` / `TryGetValue` now return `false` instead of `true` with a `null` value. An OWIN `env["StatusCodePagesOptions"]` read would throw `KeyNotFoundException` instead of returning `null`. `Items[key]` reads, including Blazor's `EndpointHtmlRenderer`, are unaffected. This needs a maintainer decision on whether the internal key's presence is a contract.

Otherwise:
- When `PathFormat` is set (re-execute), or `Items` already exists, the entry is written and removed exactly as before, with no extra feature lookups on the re-execute path.
- After `next`, the entry is still removed if `Items` was created downstream, matching the old unconditional `Remove`.
- Custom `HttpContext` implementations always take the original path.

Also adds a direct `ProjectReference` to `Microsoft.AspNetCore.Http` (for `DefaultHttpContext`). Diagnostics already depends on it through Routing, and sibling middlewares (HostFiltering, WebSockets, ResponseCaching, …) reference it the same way. No public API changes.

## Benchmark

| Default_200 (`UseStatusCodePages()`) | 334 / 327 / 327 ns (±6) | 242 / 248 / 253 ns (±3–5) | **−25%** | 1312 B | **1048 B** (middleware 288 → 24 B) |
| Default_200_NextUsesItems | 359 / 346 / 346 ns | 359 / 343 / 346 ns | — | 1312 B | 1312 B |
| ReExecute_200 (`PathFormat` set) | 332 / 326 / 353 ns | 341 / 340 / 353 ns | noise (same code path) | 1312 B | 1312 B |

  - An entry added by `next` is removed afterwards.
  - `Items` is not allocated when unused.

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md).

Removes work that `RewriteMiddleware` does on every request, even when no rule matches.

## Description

**1. Debug log arguments were computed even with Debug logging off.**
`RunRules` passed `httpContext.Request.GetEncodedUrl()` (or `Response.Headers.Location.ToString()`) to its Debug-level `LoggerMessage` calls for **every rule on every request**. The source-generated logger checks `IsEnabled` only after the arguments are evaluated, so each rule cost a full URL build (a `StringBuilder` plus strings). The calls are now guarded with `logger.IsEnabled(LogLevel.Debug)`, and the message text is unchanged when Debug is enabled.

**2. Boxed rules enumerator.** `options.Rules` is typed `IList<IRule>`, so `foreach` boxed the enumerator. It is always a `List<IRule>` (get-only, initialized), so the loop now uses the struct enumerator, with an `IList` fallback.

**3. `path.ToString().Substring(1)` for each regex rule.** `RewriteRule`, `RedirectRule` and IIS `RegexMatch` matched against a substring with the leading `/` removed. They now call `Regex.Match(path, 1, path.Length - 1)`. This gives the same match and group values; only `Group.Index` differs, and the middleware never reads it (it reads `Groups[i].Value` and `Match.Result`). The one observable difference is in `Match.Result` substitutions `$_` (whole input) and `` $` `` (text before the match). Rules whose replacement contains either token fall back to the substring path, so behavior is unchanged.

No public API changes.

## Benchmark

Local BenchmarkDotNet, 3 runs each, net12.0, 2 cores. Each op creates a `DefaultHttpContext` (`ContextOnly` = ~223 ns, 1240 B) and invokes the middleware with 3 rules that don't match (or 1 that matches) for path `/api/products/12345/details`. Debug logging is off (`NullLoggerFactory`).

### Describe the bug
Setting password length through 
```
public void ConfigureServices(IServiceCollection services){
  ...
  services.Configure<IdentityOptions>(options =>
  {
    options.Password.RequiredLength = 1;
  });
  ...
```
does not change the non-scaffolded razor page as it always says "The Password must be at least 6 and at max 100 characters long." if inputed password is < 6 characters.

### To Reproduce
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Create a new ASP.NET Core Web 2.1 application
2. Select "Web application (Model-View Controller)" 
3. Select "Change authentication"
3.1. Select "Individual User Account"
4. Select Ok to have the project scaffolded.
5. Open file Startup.cs
6. Add 
```
services.Configure<IdentityOptions>(options =>
{
  options.Password.RequiredLength = 1;
});
```

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

Issues.Title: Feedback: ensure that .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling only supported in VS 2017 and won't be supported in VS 2019
Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

Issues.Title: Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json
Issues.Body:
I used to be able to use `dotnet watch` in Visual Studio by adding the following section to `launchSettings.json` and starting the project without debugging using CTRL + F5.

```
    "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
```

This used to work in ASP.NET Core 1.1 but no longer does. According to https://github.com/aspnet/DotNetTools/issues/404 the new format for ASP.NET Core 2.0 is:

```
   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "workingDirectory": "C:\\Users\\namc\\source\\repos\\WebApplication2\\WebApplication2",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
```

The problem with this is the hard coded `executablePath` which is Windows specific and the `workingDirectory` which is specific to wherever I did a Git clone on my local machine.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json" (#1067)

Issues.Title: Nesting bug
Issues.Body:
The is a problem nesting embedded resources.  I was experimenting with nesting .cshtml files using the existing rules and did this:

Modal.cs (bootstrap modal web component)
   -> Modal.cs.cshtml (it's view file)

`Modal.cs.cshtml` is set to Embedded Resource, and clearly shows it, but is completed IGNORED by the build process (simply open the DLL in a text editor [such as Notepad++] and scroll to the bottom and look for text).  If I rename the file to "Modal.cshtml" instead it works perfectly fine!  :/  I don't think whether or not a file is embedded should have and role in excluding a file from being embedded so this seems like a bug to me.

Yes, I'm aware of upcoming nesting controls in v15.6, but I'm not able to install it yet, and regardless, this should work fine, so it should be looked into nonetheless.

Just to add: I'm using wild-cards to include the file.  If I explicitly add it I get this:

`Duplicate 'EmbeddedResource' items were included. ...`

So it's clearly found.  It's obviously something up with the build process not finding the nested file.
